ta-l1d8q3-d1e97.summary: Transitional paragraph introducing the second attribute of the divine essence treated in Distinction 8, immutability. Lombard says that only God is unchangeable and all creatures are changeable in some way. Three articles are announced: whether God is wholly immutable, whether every creature is mutable, and Augustine's modes of change.

ta-l1d8q3-d1e111.summary: First objection that God is in some way mutable. Wisdom 7:24 says wisdom is more mobile than all mobile things, and divine wisdom is God himself.
claims: Scripture calls divine wisdom the most mobile of things.

ta-l1d8q3-d1e117.summary: Second objection. Whatever moves itself is moved by itself, and Augustine says the creating Spirit moves himself, neither through time nor through place.
claims: Augustine says the Creator Spirit moves himself.

ta-l1d8q3-d1e123.summary: Third objection. What is through another reduces to what is through itself. Many things are moved by other movers, so something must be moved by itself. Every moved creature is moved by another, by God, so God is moved by himself.
claims: What is moved by another reduces to what is moved by itself.

ta-l1d8q3-d1e127.summary: Fourth objection. Whatever passes from rest into act is in some way moved (the Philosopher), since the operation of an unmoved operator is always. But God sometimes creates in act or infuses grace when he did not before, so there is at least a change from habit to act in him.
claims: Passing from inactivity to action involves change.

ta-l1d8q3-d1e130.summary: Sed contra from Malachi 3:6 ('I am God and I do not change') and James 1:17 ('with whom there is no change').
claims: Scripture affirms that God does not change.

ta-l1d8q3-d1e139.summary: Second sed contra, the Philosopher's proof. Whatever is moved is moved by another. If the mover is itself moved, it is moved by another mover, and an infinite regress is impossible. So there is a first mover that moves and is in no way moved, namely God.
claims: Whatever is moved is moved by another.
An infinite series of moved movers is impossible, so there is an unmoved first mover.

ta-l1d8q3-d1e142.summary: Thomas's determination. Every motion or change, however it is said, follows on some possibility, since motion is the act of what exists in potency. God is pure act with no admixture of potency, so there can be no change in him.
claims: All change presupposes potency.
God, as pure act, is wholly immutable.
concepts: motion as act of the potential

ta-l1d8q3-d1e145.summary: Reply to the first objection. Divine wisdom is called mobile not because it moves in itself but because it proceeds into effects, and this procession resembles motion without being motion properly. In local motion, what is in one place comes to be in another and another until the motion is complete. Similarly divine wisdom, the exemplar of things, makes its likeness in creatures in order, higher creatures first and lower ones afterward. It falls short of motion in two ways: what is in each creature is not numerically the same but a likeness, and the order is not of time but of nature, nobler creatures participating divine goodness first by nature if not by time. This is how Dionysius's talk of the Father of lights 'moving' and of divine goodness 'proceeding' into creatures is to be understood.
claims: Divine wisdom is 'mobile' only as proceeding in an order of nature into creatures by its likeness.
This procession differs from motion in that only a likeness is in each creature and the order is natural, not temporal.

ta-l1d8q3-d1e151.summary: Reply to the second objection. Augustine uses 'to be moved' broadly, as understanding and willing are a kind of movement, though properly they are operations, not motions. In this sense Plato's 'God moves himself' is true, as the Commentator says God understands and wills himself, and as we say the end moves the efficient cause. Alternatively, God moves himself in producing creatures.
claims: Understanding and willing are called motions only broadly; properly they are operations.

ta-l1d8q3-d1e158.summary: Reply to the third objection. Nothing can move itself except by distinct parts, one moving and another moved, as in an animal the soul moves and the body is moved. Nothing moves except as in act or is moved except as in potency, and both cannot belong to the same thing in the same respect. God is simple, so properly speaking he cannot move himself. The reduction of the moved-by-another to the moved-by-itself holds for reduction to the first in a genus. For the philosophers, all mobile things reduce to the first mobile, called self-moved as a composite of mover and moved, but this must be reduced further to a first simple being that is wholly immobile.
claims: Self-motion requires distinct parts, one in act and one in potency.
God, being simple, cannot properly move himself.
The self-moved first mobile must be reduced to a wholly immobile simple principle.

ta-l1d8q3-d1e161.summary: Reply to the fourth objection. Wherever operation differs from substance, there must be some motion in beginning a new operation, since an operation is acquired that was not there before. In God operation is his substance, so like his substance it is eternal. But the effect does not follow from eternity on that operation; it follows the order of wisdom, the principle of operating.
claims: In God operation is identical with substance and eternal.
God's effects are temporal by the order of his wisdom, not by any change in his operation.

ta-l1d8q3-d1e173.summary: First objection that not every creature is mutable. Every change is generation, corruption, or motion (Physics 5), and none of these is in angels and other beings separated from matter and motion, according to the philosophers.
claims: Every change is generation, corruption, or motion.
Separate substances lack all three.

ta-l1d8q3-d1e176.summary: Second objection. Whatever is mutable belongs to natural philosophy, which considers motion, and separate substances are not considered by the natural philosopher.
claims: The mutable is the subject of natural philosophy.

ta-l1d8q3-d1e179.summary: Third objection. Whatever changes is subject to change, and simple forms cannot be subjects (Boethius).
claims: Simple forms cannot be subjects.

ta-l1d8q3-d1e183.summary: Fourth objection. Lombard says every creature is moved through time or place, but some creatures have neither: the universal, which is everywhere and always (the Philosopher), and prime matter, which has no succession of times (Augustine).
claims: The universal and prime matter are not in time or place.

ta-l1d8q3-d1e186.summary: Sed contra from Psalm 101:27: you will change them and they will be changed.
claims: Scripture says creatures will be changed.

ta-l1d8q3-d1e192.summary: Second sed contra from Damascene: whatever is from nothing can turn into nothing, since what began by change must be subject to change, and every creature is such.
claims: Whatever began by change is subject to change.

ta-l1d8q3-d1e198.summary: Thomas's determination. Motion of any kind follows potency, and every creature has some potency, since only God is pure act, so all creatures are mutable and God alone immutable. There are two kinds of possibility. The first concerns what a thing has and follows from its having being from another, since nothing with being from another is necessary of itself (Avicenna) and so is possible in itself, implying dependence. This is twofold. (a) Dependence of the whole being on its source. It yields the 'vertibility into nothing' that Damascene names, but this is not properly mutability, and Augustine does not mention it. No substrate remains of which one could say it can be changed, and nothing is called possible whose contrary is necessary: creaturely being can fail only if the flow of divine goodness were withdrawn, which divine immutability makes impossible. So the creature is corruptible only conditionally, 'if left to itself' (Gregory: all would fall into nothing unless the Almighty's hand held them). (b) Dependence of part of its being, the form, presupposing matter or what stands in place of matter. This yields mutability by variation, since what is had from another can be lost of itself unless the cause's immutability prevents it. In this way the saints are immutable in glory. The second possibility follows from the creature's not being simply perfect, so that it is always open to receiving, and in this broad sense every creature is mutable, since all receiving is a kind of undergoing (to understand is a kind of undergoing, De anima 3).
claims: Every creature is mutable because every creature has some potency; God alone is pure act.
Total dependence on God yields only a conditional 'vertibility into nothing', not mutability properly speaking.
Dependence of form on a substrate yields mutability by variation, which divine immutability can prevent, as in the saints' glory.
Every creature is mutable in the broad sense of being open to further reception.

ta-l1d8q3-d1e207.summary: Reply to the first objection. The philosophers considered only change by variation of substantial or accidental form whose cause is not immutable, and they divided it into generation, corruption, and motion. Such change cannot exist in angels with respect to what is in their nature.
claims: The philosophers' division of change covers only variation of form from mutable causes.

ta-l1d8q3-d1e210.summary: Reply to the second objection, following from the first: the natural philosopher considers only that kind of change.

ta-l1d8q3-d1e214.summary: Reply to the third objection. Lombard and Augustine speak of creatures with complete being, and forms lack complete being, since they subsist not in themselves but in another. Alternatively, something is mutable either as subject of change, and in this way only what is in potency changes, or as what is removed or cast off in change, and in this way forms, which are acts, are mutable, though this does not seem to be Augustine's meaning.
claims: Forms lack complete being and change only as what is removed in change.

ta-l1d8q3-d1e217.summary: Reply to the fourth objection. Likewise, prime matter and the universal lack complete being of their own; their being is in particular composites, so they do not change per se, only per accidens, like forms.
claims: Prime matter and universals change only per accidens, having being only in composites.

ta-l1d8q3-d1e229.summary: First objection to Augustine's modes of creaturely change (through time and through place). There is change in a category only where motion is found, as in quantity or quality, and there is no motion in 'when' (the Philosopher), so creatures are not said to change through time.
claims: There is no motion in the category of 'when'.

ta-l1d8q3-d1e232.summary: Second objection. In a division one member should not be contained in another, but every motion through place is through time.
claims: Local motion is also temporal.

ta-l1d8q3-d1e235.summary: Third objection. Motion occurs in three categories (quantity, quality, place), and there is generation and corruption in substance and, in a qualified sense, in every category, all found in bodily creatures. So assigning bodily change only to place is deficient.
claims: Bodily creatures undergo motion in quantity, quality, and place, and generation and corruption.

ta-l1d8q3-d1e239.summary: Fourth objection. Time measures the first mobile, so what has no order to the motion of the first mobile has no relation to time. The soul's affections are not ordered to or subject to the motion of the heavens, so it is wrong to say that being moved through time is changing in affections.
claims: Time is the measure of the first mobile.

ta-l1d8q3-d1e242.summary: Thomas's determination. Motion properly taken has continuity and succession. As continuous it is properly measured by place, since the continuity of motion comes from the continuity of magnitude. As successive it is properly measured by time, which is the number of motion according to before and after. Some motions have both continuity and succession; others have only succession, like the motions of the affections and of thoughts, when the soul passes from one thought to another with no continuity between them. So Augustine divides creaturely change into change through place and through time.
claims: Motion has continuity, measured by place, and succession, measured by time.
Some motions, such as those of thought and affection, are successive without continuity.

ta-l1d8q3-d1e245.summary: Reply to the first objection. There is no motion in the category 'when' as a terminus, since no motion terminates in a when as it does in a where, but there is motion in 'when' as in a measure.
claims: 'When' is a measure of motion, not its terminus.

ta-l1d8q3-d1e248.summary: Reply to the second objection. The division is to be understood by precision: some change is through place and time, some through time only.
claims: The division contrasts change through place and time with change through time alone.

ta-l1d8q3-d1e251.summary: Reply to the third objection. Although there are many bodily motions, all are ordered to the local motion of the heavens, the cause of all bodily motion, so local motion covers them all. Alternatively, motions other than local motion are covered by change through time, since only local motion is simply continuous (the Commentator), and Augustine says God moves bodily creatures both through time and through place.
claims: All bodily motions are ordered to the heavens' local motion.
Only local motion is simply continuous.

ta-l1d8q3-d1e254.summary: Reply to the fourth objection. 'Time' is said in two ways. In one, it is the number of before and after in the motion of the heavens, continuous through motion and magnitude, measuring whatever is ordered to that motion, per se (bodily motions) or per accidens (soul operations related to the body); this is the philosophers' sense. In the other, more common sense, it is the number of anything with before and after, so that time measures the intellect's successive simple conceptions. This time need not be continuous, since what it measures is not continuous. This is the sense used here and often by theologians.
claims: Time is either the continuous number of the heavens' motion or, more broadly, the number of any succession, including discontinuous thoughts.
Theologians often use 'time' in the broader, non-continuous sense.

ta-l1d8q3-d1e264.summary: An expositio textus on Distinction 8's account of divine truth, immutability, and simplicity. (1) Lombard names only three attributes because they concern the perfection of divine being as perfect being: truth or propriety excludes privation and non-being, immutability excludes potentiality, and simplicity expresses the integrity of being, since whatever is in the simple is its own being. (2) 'Nature, substance, essence' are synonyms here: nature as the form following the whole, substance as the first predicament opposed to accident, essence as not existing in a subject. (3) Deriving 'essence' from 'esse' as 'wisdom' from 'sapere' follows the order of our knowledge, which reaches habits from acts. (4) 'Who is more than he who said I am who am?': being admits more and less not in the participated nature but in the mode of participating, as an angel is more intellectual than a human. (5) God has no experiential knowledge of past and future, since he does not undergo the succession of times. (6) 'Our being compared to his is nothing': compared as to its source, our being exists only through that comparison; compared by proportion, it is as nothing, being infinitely distant. (7) 'Being is not an accident to God': being 'accidental' to every created quiddity, in the sense of not belonging to its concept, since one can understand humanity and doubt whether a man exists. (8) Hilary's 'subsistent truth, abiding cause, natural property of the genus' excludes three imperfections of creaturely being: it does not subsist of itself, it is caused and potential, and it differs from the quiddity, whereas God's being is God subsisting, the immutable cause of all being, and his very quiddity.
claims: Truth, immutability, and simplicity express the perfection of divine being by excluding non-being, potency, and composition.
Being admits degrees in the mode of participation, not in the participated nature.
Being is 'accidental' to every created quiddity in that it falls outside its concept.
Divine being is subsistent, uncaused and immutable, and identical with the divine quiddity.
concepts: real distinction of essence and esse

ta-l1d8q3-Dd1e92.summary: The Prooemium of Question 3 introduces the second divine attribute of Distinction 8, immutability, and announces three articles: God's immutability, creatures' mutability, and Augustine's modes of change.

ta-l1d8q3-Dd1e103.summary: Article 1 asks whether God is wholly immutable. Objections cite the mobility of wisdom, Augustine's and Plato's self-moving God, the reduction to a self-mover, and God's new acts. Thomas holds that all change follows potency, so God, as pure act, is wholly immutable. The replies explain wisdom's 'mobility' as an ordered, quasi-motive procession of its likeness into creatures, natural rather than temporal. They treat understanding and willing as operations rather than motions, and show that self-motion requires composition and that the self-moved first mobile reduces to an immobile simple principle. God's operation is eternal and identical with his substance, while its effects are temporal by the order of wisdom.
claims: God is wholly immutable as pure act.
God's eternal operation produces temporal effects according to the order of his wisdom.

ta-l1d8q3-Dd1e165.summary: Article 2 asks whether every creature is mutable. Against the philosophers' view that separate substances are changeless, Thomas holds that every creature has some potency and so is mutable. He distinguishes possibility from dependence of the whole being, which yields only a conditional 'vertibility into nothing' prevented by divine immutability, and possibility from dependence of form on a substrate, which yields variation. He also counts the creature's openness to further perfection as mutability broadly taken. The philosophers' division of change covers only variation of form from mutable causes. Forms, prime matter, and universals change only per accidens.
claims: Every creature is mutable because it has potency; God alone is immutable.
A creature's total dependence yields only conditional, not proper, mutability.
The saints in glory are immutable through God's immutable will.

ta-l1d8q3-Dd1e221.summary: Article 3 defends Augustine's division of creaturely change into change through place and change through time. Motion has continuity, measured by place, and succession, measured by time. Bodily motions have both, while spiritual motions of thought and affection have succession only. All bodily motions are ordered to the heavens' local motion. Theologians use 'time' broadly, for the number of any succession, including the discontinuous succession of thoughts, beyond the philosophers' continuous time of the heavens.
claims: Change through place and time covers bodily motion; change through time alone covers spiritual motion.
'Time' in theology includes discrete succession, such as of thoughts.

ta-l1d8q3-Dd1e259.summary: The Expositio textus of Distinction 8 explains why Lombard names truth, immutability, and simplicity as the perfections of divine being and glosses 'nature, substance, essence'. It covers degrees of being by mode of participation and the 'nothingness' of our being by proportion to God's. It also discusses the sense in which being is 'accidental' to created quiddities but not to God, and Hilary's characterization of divine being as subsistent, causal, and identical with the divine quiddity.
claims: Being is accidental to created quiddities in falling outside their concept, but is God's quiddity.
Truth, immutability, and simplicity exclude non-being, potency, and composition from divine being.

ta-l1d8q3.summary: Quaestio 3 of Book I, Distinction 8 treats divine immutability and creaturely mutability. Article 1 holds that God, as pure act, is wholly immutable. Wisdom's 'mobility' is the ordered, non-temporal procession of its likeness into creatures, and God's eternal operation, identical with his substance, yields temporal effects by the order of wisdom. Article 2 holds that every creature is mutable because every creature has potency. Total dependence on God yields only a conditional 'vertibility into nothing' that divine immutability prevents, while dependence of form on substrate yields mutability by variation. Article 3 defends Augustine's division of change into through place and through time, grounded in the continuity and succession of motion, with a broader theological sense of time covering discontinuous spiritual succession. The Expositio explains why truth, immutability, and simplicity constitute the perfection of divine being and how divine being, unlike created being, is identical with its quiddity.
claims: God alone is immutable, as pure act; every creature is mutable through potency.
Creatures' total dependence on God makes them corruptible only conditionally.
Change through place and through time corresponds to the continuity and succession of motion.
Divine being alone is subsistent and identical with its quiddity.
